topics.name: A Streetcar Named Desire
topics.kicker: Tennessee Williams’s 1947 play · Old Southern gentility meets raw desire
topics.briefing: _A Streetcar Named Desire_ follows Blanche DuBois, a fading Southern belle who moves into her sister Stella’s cramped New Orleans apartment after losing the family estate. Blanche’s fragile fantasies collide with the raw, physical world of Stella’s husband, Stanley Kowalski, to the sound of a blues piano drifting in from a nearby bar. Tennessee Williams’s play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama and later became a landmark film starring Marlon Brando.

sample.note: 11 real QBReader tossups (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 8 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: Hart Crane’s poem “The Broken Tower” serves as the epigraph to this play, whose brother-in-law character cites the Napoleonic Code while rifling through a trunk he suspects hides money stolen from a property sale.
tossups.r: Stage directions call for ambient “blue piano” music drifting in from a nearby bar throughout this play. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play in which Blanche DuBois visits her sister Stella in New Orleans.

tossups.p: One character in this play recalls feeling thrilled when her husband smashed every lightbulb in their apartment with the heel of her slipper on their wedding night. Her visiting sister claims a wealthy old admirer named Shep Huntleigh is taking her on a cruise, and jokes that she will die one day eating an unwashed grape.
tossups.r: That visiting sister is eventually led away to a mental hospital. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about Blanche DuBois’s stay with Stella and Stanley Kowalski.

tossups.p: Unpaid debts cost this play’s heroine her family’s estate, Belle Reve, forcing her to move into her sister’s small New Orleans apartment. She covers a bare lightbulb with a paper lantern and takes long baths throughout the play to calm her nerves.
tossups.r: She eventually says she has always depended on “the kindness of strangers.” For 10 points, name this play in which Blanche DuBois moves in with Stanley and Stella Kowalski.

tossups.p: Before the action of this play begins, its heroine loses her teaching job and is asked to leave a hotel back in Laurel, Mississippi, amid rumors about her behavior. Years before that, her young husband died by suicide after she discovered him with another man.
tossups.r: She arrives in New Orleans a fragile wreck, dependent on her sister Stella’s charity. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about Blanche DuBois.

tossups.p: A poker buddy named Mitch courts this play’s heroine for much of its running time, but drops his plans to marry her after her brother-in-law tells him about her past in Laurel. That brother-in-law, enraged during an earlier poker night, had thrown a radio out of a window.
tossups.r: He later assaults her while his pregnant wife is away at the hospital. For 10 points, name this play in which Blanche DuBois stays with her sister and brother-in-law in New Orleans.

tossups.p: Elia Kazan directed both the original 1947 Broadway production and the 1951 film version of this play, each starring Marlon Brando as its loutish, physical antagonist. That same film cast Vivien Leigh in the lead role originally played onstage by Jessica Tandy.
tossups.r: This play won the 1948 Pulitzer Prize for Drama. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about a fading Southern belle named Blanche DuBois.

tossups.p: This play’s heroine disparages her brother-in-law’s Polish immigrant background as common, even as her own sister finds his physical, hot-tempered nature thrilling. That sister ultimately chooses to believe her husband’s version of events over her own visiting sister’s.
tossups.r: As a result, the visiting sister is sent away to an institution. For 10 points, name this play starring the sisters Blanche DuBois and Stella Kowalski.

tossups.p: Much of this play takes place in a cramped apartment on Elysian Fields Avenue in New Orleans’s French Quarter. Its heroine arrives there with nowhere else to go, having lost her ancestral home to debt.
tossups.r: She spends the play clashing with her brutish brother-in-law, Stanley Kowalski. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about Blanche DuBois’s visit to her sister Stella.

tossups.p: Stanley Kowalski’s regular poker buddies in this play include men named Steve and Pablo, along with his friend Mitch. During one especially heated poker night, Stanley throws a radio out of a window in anger at his sister-in-law.
tossups.r: That sister-in-law, Blanche, had kept turning on the radio while he played cards. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play set in New Orleans.

tossups.p: Long before this play begins, its heroine’s young husband took his own life after she discovered him involved with another man, a loss that haunts her for the rest of the story. She arrives in New Orleans still clinging to an old-fashioned, genteel idea of herself.
tossups.r: That self-image clashes badly with her brother-in-law’s blunt, modern manner. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about the visiting Blanche DuBois.

tossups.p: The literal New Orleans trolley line that once carried riders toward this play’s setting inspired its title, a detail Tennessee Williams turns into the play’s central symbol for its heroine’s downfall. That heroine arrives by trolley at her sister’s apartment, suitcase in hand.
tossups.r: She soon clashes with her brother-in-law, a brutish war veteran named Stanley Kowalski. For 10 points, name this play about Blanche DuBois’s visit to New Orleans.

tossups.p: This play’s heroine covers a bare lightbulb in her sister’s apartment with a Chinese paper lantern, unable to bear being seen in a harsh, honest light. She also takes long, frequent baths throughout the play, as if trying to wash something away.
tossups.r: Her fragile hold on reality finally breaks after her brother-in-law assaults her one night. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about Blanche DuBois.

tossups.p: This play contrasts its heroine’s fading Old South refinement with the raw, modern vitality of the working-class city around her. Its heroine is a former high school English teacher who clings to illusions of elegance despite having nowhere left to live.
tossups.r: She leans on the generosity of her sister Stella and brother-in-law Stanley for a place to stay. For 10 points, name this play about Blanche DuBois’s arrival in New Orleans.

tossups.p: At the end of this play, its heroine is led away by a doctor, telling him she has always depended on “the kindness of strangers.” Her sister Stella chooses to stay with her husband rather than fully believe her sister’s accusations.
tossups.r: That final scene follows months of tension in a cramped New Orleans apartment. For 10 points, name this Tennessee Williams play about Blanche DuBois’s breakdown.

tossups.p: This play follows a fragile Southern woman who moves in with her sister and brother-in-law in a small New Orleans apartment after losing her family’s home. Tension between her old-fashioned manners and her brother-in-law’s rough temper builds throughout the story.
tossups.r: Tennessee Williams’s play won the 1948 Pulitzer Prize for Drama and was later made into a famous film. For 10 points, name this play about Blanche DuBois, Stella, and Stanley Kowalski.

trap.title: Which Williams play is it?
trap.body: Tennessee Williams wrote several Southern-set tragedies, so clues about a fragile woman or a hot, cramped apartment could mean _The Glass Menagerie_ or _Cat on a Hot Tin Roof_ instead. The word “Desire” can also pull in Eugene O’Neill’s unrelated play _Desire Under the Elms_.
trap.fix: Check the names: Blanche DuBois, Stella, Stanley Kowalski, and Mitch in New Orleans mean this play. And if you’re asked to “name this play,” the answer is the title — not “Blanche DuBois.”
trap.line: Real answer line: A Streetcar Named Desire.

topics.name: Beowulf
topics.kicker: Old English epic poem · Earliest great hero story in the English language
topics.briefing: _Beowulf_ is the oldest surviving epic poem in English, and nobody knows who wrote it — only one battered medieval copy survived, and it was almost lost again in a fire. Its hero sails from the land of the Geats to rescue the aging Danish king Hrothgar from a monster terrorizing his mead-hall, then returns home to fight one final dragon fifty years later.

media.note: Study guide: key facts (setting, genre, climax), background, and a link to the full summary

qb.tip: All 14 are about the hero, not his victims — the dragon-and-Wiglaf ending and the fight with Grendel at Heorot are the two clues almost every packet uses.

sample.note: the 14 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: J. R. R. Tolkien’s 1936 lecture “The Monsters and the Critics” helped convince scholars that this poem deserved serious study as literature. It survives in just one damaged manuscript, the Nowell Codex, later singed by fire, and its unnamed narrator is called a “scop” [“shop”], an Old English term for a court poet.
tossups.r: This poem opens with the funeral of the legendary Danish king Scyld Scefing [“shild SHAY-ving”]. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose hero kills the monster Grendel.

tossups.p: Unferth [“OON-ferth”] taunts the title character over a boyhood swimming match against a man named Breca, but later lends him his own sword, Hrunting [“HROON-ting”]. That blade fails when its new owner dives into a lake to fight a vengeful female monster.
tossups.r: Years later, the hero’s young kinsman Wiglaf [“WIG-lahf”] is the only one who stands with him against a treasure-guarding dragon. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose hero kills Grendel and Grendel’s mother.

tossups.p: For twelve years, a demon described as a descendant of the biblical Cain terrorizes King Hrothgar’s [“ROTH-gar’s”] mead-hall by dragging off and devouring sleeping warriors at night. Hearing of these attacks across the sea, a Geatish [“GAY-ish”] warrior sails to Denmark with a band of thanes to offer his help.
tossups.r: That warrior rips the demon’s arm from its socket after an overnight wrestling match in the hall called Heorot [“HAY-oh-roht”]. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem in which the hero defeats the monster Grendel.

tossups.p: Furious after her son’s death, a monster described as a “water-witch” drags off King Hrothgar’s counselor Aeschere [“ASH-heh-ray”] in revenge. The title hero dives into her lake lair, where his borrowed sword Hrunting fails him, forcing him to grab a giant’s blade hanging on the wall.
tossups.r: With that ancient sword, he kills the creature and returns to the surface carrying Grendel’s head as a trophy. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose hero kills both Grendel and Grendel’s mother.

tossups.p: Fifty years after becoming king of the Geats, this poem’s protagonist faces one final monster: a dragon enraged after a thief steals a cup from its barrow. Only his young kinsman Wiglaf stays to help him, and the hero’s own sword shatters against the dragon’s head.
tossups.r: Mortally wounded, he names Wiglaf his successor before dying, and his people build him a tall barrow by the sea. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem about a Geatish hero who dies fighting a dragon.

tossups.p: This poem opens with the ship-funeral of a legendary Danish king named Scyld Scefing [“shild SHAY-ving”], generations before its main story begins. Its hero serves the Geatish king Hygelac [“HIH-geh-lahk”], and later becomes king himself after both Hygelac and his son Heardred [“HEH-ar-red”] die.
tossups.r: That hero’s own funeral closes the poem, one of three funeral scenes in the text. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem about a warrior who slays Grendel.

tossups.p: Queen Wealhtheow [“WAIL-thay-oh”] presents a jeweled cup to this poem’s protagonist at a welcoming feast in Heorot. King Hrothgar had once paid a blood-debt on behalf of the hero’s late father, Ecgtheow [“EDGE-thay-oh”], which is partly why the hero feels obligated to help him now.
tossups.r: That hero then uses his bare hands, refusing a weapon, to tear off a monster’s arm. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose protagonist defeats Grendel at Hrothgar’s mead-hall.

tossups.p: A court poet entertains Heorot’s [“HAY-oh-rohts”] hall with a tragic song about Finn, a Frisian king caught in a deadly feud, shortly after the hero’s first triumph. This poem famously opens with the hard-to-translate word “Hwaet!” [“hwaht”], which one celebrated modern translation renders simply as “So.”
tossups.r: That translation, by the Nobel Prize–winning poet Seamus Heaney [“SHAY-mus HEE-nee”], made this poem newly popular with readers. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem about a hero who kills the monster Grendel.

tossups.p: As he dies, this poem’s hero gives a golden collar to his one loyal companion, Wiglaf, son of Weohstan [“WAY-oh-stahn”], and asks to see the treasure he has won. Decades earlier, that same hero had raced a rival named Breca in a swimming match, though a jealous courtier claimed Breca won.
tossups.r: Wiglaf then scolds the warriors who abandoned their king during his final battle. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose title Geatish hero dies fighting a dragon.

tossups.p: Described as a descendant of the biblical Cain, a monster bursts into a mead-hall and carries off thirty sleeping thanes, launching twelve years of nightly terror. After tearing off its arm bare-handed, this poem’s hero hangs the limb from the rafters as a trophy.
tossups.r: The monster’s mother soon attacks in revenge for her son’s death. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem in which a Geatish hero defeats Grendel and his mother.

tossups.p: This poem’s protagonist claims he once killed nine sea-monsters during a days-long swimming contest with a man named Breca, a story a jealous courtier named Unferth [“OON-ferth”] doubts at a Danish feast. Unferth later lends this hero a sword that fails against an underwater foe.
tossups.r: That hero had sailed from the land of the Geats to rid Heorot of a demon. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose hero kills the monster Grendel.

tossups.p: A single escaped slave disturbs an ancient barrow and steals a golden cup, waking the dragon guarding it and setting up this poem’s final battle. This poem’s aging hero, now a Geatish king, attacks the dragon alongside Wiglaf after his retainers flee in terror.
tossups.r: The dragon’s poisoned bite ultimately kills the hero even though he strikes a fatal blow in return. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem about a hero who dies fighting a dragon.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero once swam home across the sea carrying thirty suits of armor after a disastrous raid killed his king, Hygelac [“HIH-geh-lahk”]. He later refuses the Geatish throne himself, serving instead as a guardian to young Heardred [“HEH-ar-red”], Hygelac’s son.
tossups.r: Only after Heardred also dies in battle does this hero finally accept the crown. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem about a loyal Geatish warrior who kills Grendel.

tossups.p: King Hrothgar builds a magnificent mead-hall to celebrate his military victories, naming it Heorot [“HAY-oh-roht”] for the hart antlers that decorate its gables. His pride is short-lived once a swamp-dwelling demon, enraged by the hall’s nightly singing and laughter, begins stalking its warriors.
tossups.r: A Geatish hero crosses the sea to end those attacks. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem whose hero kills the monster Grendel at Heorot.

tossups.p: This poem’s hero spends his final years as a respected king of the Geats, decades after his famous victories as a young warrior in Denmark. When a dragon begins terrorizing his kingdom after its treasure is disturbed, he arms himself for one last fight.
tossups.r: His kinsman Wiglaf [“WIG-lahf”] is the only warrior brave enough to help him battle the dragon, which kills him in the end. For 10 points, name this Old English epic poem about a hero who also killed Grendel and his mother.

clues.t: Kills the monster Grendel, who has been terrorizing King Hrothgar’s mead-hall by night
Grendel’s target is Heorot, the great mead-hall built by the Danish king Hrothgar
Dies in old age fighting a dragon, helped only by his young kinsman Wiglaf
The oldest surviving major poem in Old English; its author is unknown
Also kills Grendel’s mother in her underwater lair, after his borrowed sword fails him
Hrothgar is the aging Danish king who asks this Geatish hero for help
Unferth lends him the sword Hrunting, which fails against Grendel’s mother
Boasts of a boyhood swimming match against Breca, which Unferth doubts at a feast
A warrior of the Geats loyal to King Hygelac; after Hygelac’s son also dies, he becomes king himself
J. R. R. Tolkien’s lecture “The Monsters and the Critics” made scholars take this poem seriously
Seamus Heaney’s modern English translation introduced this poem to many new readers
Opens with the hard-to-translate Old English word “Hwaet!,” often rendered as “Listen!” or “So.”
Opens with the ship-funeral of the legendary Danish king Scyld Scefing, generations before the main plot
Queen Wealhtheow welcomes him with a jeweled cup at a feast in Heorot
His late father, Ecgtheow, once had a blood-debt settled by King Hrothgar himself
Grendel’s mother kills Hrothgar’s trusted counselor Aeschere in revenge for her son’s death
His one loyal helper against the dragon, Wiglaf, is identified as the son of Weohstan
A court poet sings of Finn, a Frisian king caught in a tragic feud, during a victory feast
Dying, he gives his golden collar to Wiglaf and asks to see the dragon’s treasure one last time
Narrated by an unnamed “scop,” the Old English word for a court poet or singer
Grendel is described as a monstrous descendant of the biblical murderer Cain
Survives in only one damaged medieval manuscript, the Nowell Codex, later singed by fire

trap.title: Hero, monster, or king?
trap.body: _Beowulf_ names the Geatish hero, not any of the characters he interacts with. Grendel and Grendel’s mother are the monsters he kills, Hrothgar is the aged Danish king he rescues, and Wiglaf is the loyal kinsman who helps him kill the dragon at the end of his life.
trap.fix: If the clue describes a victim, a king being helped, or a sidekick, don’t buzz with that character’s name — the answer is always the hero himself, Beowulf.

topics.name: The Catcher in the Rye
topics.kicker: J. D. Salinger’s 1951 novel · Teen alienation in one unforgettable voice
topics.briefing: _The Catcher in the Rye_ follows sixteen-year-old Holden Caulfield during a restless few days in New York City after he is expelled from his prep school, Pencey Prep. J. D. Salinger tells the whole story in Holden’s own slangy, cynical voice as he dodges “phonies,” wanders the city alone, and aches for his little sister Phoebe and his dead younger brother Allie. The novel became one of the most read — and most banned — books in American schools.

qb.tip: All 9 giveaways end on Holden Caulfield’s name or “by J. D. Salinger” — Pencey Prep, Phoebe, and the ducks in Central Park are the most reused clues.

sample.note: the 9 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One chapter of this novel reworks J. D. Salinger’s own earlier short story “Slight Rebellion Off Madison.” Its narrator tells the whole story while recovering someplace out West under a psychoanalyst’s care, and he flees his former English teacher Mr. Antolini’s apartment after waking to find the man patting his head.
tossups.r: That narrator also loses his fencing team’s equipment on a New York City subway car. For 10 points, name this novel narrated by Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator plays pinball with dormmates named Ackley and Brossard before getting into a fistfight with his roommate, Stradlater, over a girl named Jane Gallagher. Before that fight, he writes Stradlater’s English composition for him, describing a baseball glove covered in poems.
tossups.r: That glove belonged to the narrator’s late younger brother. For 10 points, name this novel in which Holden Caulfield is expelled from Pencey Prep.

tossups.p: At the Edmont Hotel, this novel’s narrator accepts the elevator operator Maurice’s five-dollar offer to send a young woman named Sunny to his room, though the awkward visit goes nowhere. Maurice later punches him in the stomach while Sunny takes extra money from his wallet.
tossups.r: The same narrator buys a red hunting cap in New York and wears it backward. For 10 points, name this novel about Holden Caulfield’s wandering weekend after leaving Pencey Prep.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator is shunned by his school’s fencing team after he leaves their foils and equipment behind on a subway car. He is also expelled from his Pennsylvania boarding school for failing four out of five classes.
tossups.r: He spends the following weekend wandering alone through New York City rather than go straight home. For 10 points, name this novel narrated by the teenager Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator resents his older brother D. B. for “selling out” as a screenwriter in Hollywood after once writing a short story the narrator admired. Throughout the book, that narrator constantly complains about “phonies,” people he sees as fake or hypocritical.
tossups.r: He misses his late younger brother Allie and dotes on his little sister Phoebe. For 10 points, name this novel by J. D. Salinger.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator visits his former English teacher, Mr. Antolini, late one night for advice, only to flee in alarm after the man pats his head while he sleeps on the couch. Confused and exhausted, the narrator spends the rest of that night on a bench in Grand Central Station.
tossups.r: Earlier that night, he had sneaked home to see his sister, Phoebe. For 10 points, name this novel whose narrator is expelled from Pencey Prep.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator repeatedly asks cab drivers where the ducks on a frozen Central Park lagoon go every winter. He also drops and breaks a rare record, “Little Shirley Beans,” that he bought as a gift for his little sister.
tossups.r: That sister, Phoebe, later talks him out of running away, and he watches her ride a carousel. For 10 points, name this novel starring Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator grows furious imagining his roommate Stradlater on a date with a girl named Jane Gallagher, whom he remembers fondly for the way she kept all her kings in the back row while playing checkers. The resulting fistfight leaves him with a bloody face.
tossups.r: He had already lost his school’s fencing equipment on the subway that same day. For 10 points, name this novel about Holden Caulfield’s expulsion from Pencey Prep.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator keeps a baseball glove covered in poems written in green ink by his brother Allie, who died of leukemia years earlier. He once broke his hand punching out the garage windows the night Allie died.
tossups.r: That narrator also treasures a record called “Little Shirley Beans” that he buys for his sister Phoebe. For 10 points, name this novel narrated by Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: Near the end of this novel, its narrator sits in the rain outside a carousel, crying from happiness while watching his little sister reach for the gold ring as she rides. Earlier that day, he had planned to run away out West and live alone in a cabin.
tossups.r: He never fully explains to readers why he is telling this whole story from some kind of rest facility. For 10 points, name this novel narrated by Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator loves the Museum of Natural History specifically because its glass dioramas never change, unlike everything else in his life. He contrasts this permanence with his own confusion about growing up, which he associates with phoniness and loss.
tossups.r: He imagines a job standing in a field of grain, catching children before they tumble off a steep, unseen cliff nearby. For 10 points, name this novel about Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: This novel opens at Pencey Prep, a Pennsylvania boarding school its narrator is about to leave for good after failing most of his classes. He first visits his elderly history teacher, Mr. Spencer, to say an awkward goodbye.
tossups.r: He then takes a train to New York City instead of going straight home to tell his parents. For 10 points, name this novel about Holden Caulfield’s expulsion.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator brags that his precocious little sister has gotten all A’s, joking that he is the only dumb one in the family. He also resents his older brother, D. B., a once-promising writer now working in the movie business.
tossups.r: That narrator secretly visits his sister’s school to leave her a note, since he plans to run away before she comes home. For 10 points, name this novel whose narrator is Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: This novel’s narrator addresses the reader directly from a rest home, where a psychoanalyst keeps asking whether he will apply himself at school. He refuses to tell his whole life story, starting instead from his last day at a Pennsylvania prep school.
tossups.r: Over the following rainy weekend, he wanders alone through New York City, calling nearly everyone he meets a phony. For 10 points, name this novel about Holden Caulfield.

tossups.p: The teenage narrator of this novel is expelled from yet another boarding school, Pencey Prep, just before Christmas break. Rather than go home immediately, he spends a lonely few days wandering around New York City.
tossups.r: He constantly complains about “phonies” and desperately misses his little sister, Phoebe, and his dead brother, Allie. For 10 points, name this novel by J. D. Salinger narrated by Holden Caulfield.

clues.t: Expelled from Pencey Prep, a Pennsylvania boarding school, at the very start of the novel
Deeply loves his practical little sister Phoebe, who talks him out of running away for good
Constantly complains that almost everyone he meets is a “phony”
J. D. Salinger’s only published novel, narrated entirely in its teenage hero’s own slangy voice
His younger brother Allie died of leukemia; he keeps Allie’s baseball glove, covered in poems
His roommate Stradlater fights with him after a date with a girl named Jane Gallagher
Keeps wondering where the ducks in Central Park’s frozen lagoon go every winter
Flees his former teacher Mr. Antolini’s apartment after the man pats his head while he sleeps

topics.briefing: _Les Misérables_ follows Jean Valjean, a Frenchman jailed nineteen years for stealing a loaf of bread, whose life is transformed when a bishop repays his crime with mercy instead of punishment. Hunted for decades afterward by the relentless police inspector Javert, Valjean rescues a dying woman’s daughter, Cosette, and raises her as his own. Victor Hugo’s sprawling 1862 novel builds to the barricades of Paris, where a band of student revolutionaries make a doomed last stand.

tossups.r: There, the protagonist decides that “we must cultivate our garden” rather than keep debating philosophy. For 10 points, name this Voltaire novella that mocks blind optimism.

tossups.p: A kind Anabaptist named Jacques dies saving a sailor’s life during a shipwreck that strands this novel’s protagonist in Portugal. He arrives just as the real 1755 earthquake strikes Lisbon, which his tutor Pangloss insists is still somehow for the best.
tossups.r: The two are then punished at a public ceremony called an auto-da-fé. For 10 points, name this Voltaire novella about a relentlessly optimistic young man.

tossups.p: Gold and jewels are considered worthless in a hidden kingdom that this novel’s protagonist visits with his servant Cacambo. Earlier, that protagonist and Cacambo narrowly escape being killed by the Oreillons, who mistake them for Jesuits.
tossups.r: The protagonist leaves that hidden kingdom, El Dorado, riding treasure-laden sheep. For 10 points, name this Voltaire novella about a relentlessly optimistic young man.

tossups.p: A Venetian nobleman named Pococurante tells this novel’s protagonist that he hates nearly every book and painting in his own famous collection. Later, six kings who have all lost their thrones share a dinner together in Venice with that same protagonist.
tossups.r: The protagonist ends the novel deciding that “we must cultivate our garden.” For 10 points, name this satirical novella by Voltaire.

tossups.p: This novel opens at the castle of Thunder-ten-Tronckh, where a tutor named Pangloss teaches that this is “the best of all possible worlds.” This novel’s protagonist is soon expelled for kissing Cunégonde and is swept into a war between the Bulgars and the Abars.
tossups.r: He later reunites with Pangloss, who survived a public execution ceremony called an auto-da-fé. For 10 points, name this Voltaire novella about a relentlessly optimistic young man.

tossups.p: Voltaire wrote this novel to mock the real philosopher Gottfried Leibniz’s claim that everything happens for the best. Its full title adds the subtitle “or, Optimism,” and it was published quickly and anonymously in 1759.
tossups.r: The novel famously ends with the advice that “we must cultivate our garden.” For 10 points, name this short satirical novella about a relentlessly optimistic young man.

trap.title: Don’t name the author!
trap.body: A tossup that says “name this novel” or “name this satire” wants the title, Candide, not the author, Voltaire — even though Voltaire comes up constantly in clues about the Enlightenment. Pangloss and Leibniz, the philosophers behind the “best of all possible worlds” idea this book mocks, are also easy to blurt out by mistake.
trap.fix: Train yourself to answer with the title whenever you hear “name this novel/satire/work.” If the clues describe a philosopher’s optimistic ideas being mocked, that’s Pangloss or Leibniz — not the answer itself.

topics.briefing: Deep in a forest outside Athens, the fairy king Oberon and his queen Titania are in the middle of a marriage spat, and the mischievous sprite Puck is about to make it much worse. A magic flower meant to fix one couple’s love life ends up on the wrong eyelids, a boastful weaver named Bottom is given a donkey’s head, and everyone falls for the wrong person. _A Midsummer Night’s Dream_ is one of Shakespeare’s most performed comedies.

tossups.p: This play’s trickster sprite boasts that he can disguise himself as “a roasted crab” or a “three-foot stool” to play pranks on old women. Later, that same character smears a magic flower’s juice on the wrong Athenian’s eyelids, making him fall for the wrong woman.
tossups.r: A weaver named Nick Bottom is given a donkey’s head after rehearsing a play about Pyramus and Thisbe with his fellow “rude mechanicals.” For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy in which Puck’s mischief confuses two pairs of young lovers.

tossups.p: In one speech, a character claims that “the lunatic, the lover, and the poet are of imagination all compact.” That same character, the Duke of Athens, presides over the wedding that frames this play’s action.
tossups.r: In the forest outside his city, four young Athenians get tangled up after the fairy Puck mistakenly enchants the wrong man’s eyes with a love potion, and a weaver named Bottom is transformed so that he has a donkey’s head. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the fairy king Oberon and his queen Titania.

tossups.p: This play’s final speech begs the audience’s pardon, beginning “If we shadows have offended, think but this, and all is mended.” Earlier, the same speaker gleefully says, “Lord, what fools these mortals be!” as the enchanted Athenian lovers approach.
tossups.r: That mischievous fairy, Puck, had put a love potion on Lysander’s eyes, and Oberon had enchanted Demetrius’s, so both men chased Helena instead of Hermia. A weaver named Nick Bottom is given a donkey’s head while rehearsing a play with his fellow “rude mechanicals.” For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy set partly in an enchanted forest.

tossups.p: One character promises, “I go, I go; look how I go, swifter than arrow from the Tartar’s bow,” before carrying out a fairy king’s orders. That king, Oberon, wants the juice of a magic flower applied to his queen Titania’s eyes so she will fall for the first creature she sees.
tossups.r: That creature turns out to be Nick Bottom, a weaver whose head has just been turned into a donkey’s. Meanwhile, four young Athenians get hopelessly confused after the same potion is applied to the wrong pair of eyes. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the trickster sprite Puck.

tossups.p: During the mechanicals’ performance, the actor playing a lion assures the audience that he is really just Snug the joiner. Other members of that acting troupe play a wall and the moonlight in the same production.
tossups.r: Led by Peter Quince, the “rude mechanicals” perform the tragedy of Pyramus and Thisbe at a royal wedding. Earlier, in the forest, Puck’s love-potion mix-up leaves Helena pursued by both Lysander and Demetrius. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy in which weaver Nick Bottom is transformed with a donkey’s head.

tossups.p: Early in this play, a father demands that Athenian law be used to punish his daughter for refusing an arranged marriage; unless she obeys, she faces death or life in a convent. That daughter, Hermia, flees into the forest with her true love instead.
tossups.r: There, the fairy king Oberon orders Puck to use a magic flower’s juice to fix a mortal’s love troubles, but Puck enchants the wrong young man, making both Athenian suitors chase Helena. A weaver named Bottom is given a donkey’s head. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the fairy queen Titania.

tossups.p: Before this play begins, one character had abandoned his engagement to Helena after falling for her friend Hermia instead, which is why Helena now chases him into the forest. There, the fairy Puck’s meddling with a magic potion only deepens the confusion between the two couples.
tossups.r: Meanwhile, the fairy king Oberon wants to use the same flower’s juice to punish his queen Titania, who ends up falling in love with a donkey-headed weaver. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy that ends with a triple wedding in Athens.

tossups.p: This play’s fairy queen commands servants named Peaseblossom, Cobweb, Moth, and Mustardseed. She is tricked by her husband Oberon into falling in love with a weaver whose head has been turned into a donkey’s.
tossups.r: That weaver, Nick Bottom, had been rehearsing a tragedy about Pyramus and Thisbe with his fellow “rude mechanicals” when Puck transformed him. Meanwhile, four young Athenians get mixed up by the same magic flower. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the fairy queen Titania.

tossups.p: This play’s fairy king wants to win custody of a changeling Indian boy away from his wife, so he sends his servant to fetch a magic flower called “love-in-idleness.” That servant, Puck, fetches the flower, whose juice soon causes trouble far beyond the fairy queen.
tossups.r: Puck accidentally enchants Lysander instead of Demetrius, making both young men chase Helena through the forest, and he also gives a weaver named Bottom the head of a donkey. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy in which the fairy king Oberon and queen Titania feud over a changeling boy.

tossups.p: Scholars think Shakespeare wrote this comedy around 1595, possibly for an aristocratic wedding celebration, and its earliest printed text, a First Quarto, appeared in 1600. The play follows four young Athenian lovers whose night in an enchanted forest is thrown into chaos by a fairy’s magic love potion.
tossups.r: That trickster, Puck, causes most of the trouble, including transforming a weaver named Nick Bottom so that he wears a donkey’s head. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the fairy monarchs Oberon and Titania.

tossups.p: This play’s six “rude mechanicals” include a tinker, a joiner, a bellows-mender, and a tailor. Led by Peter Quince, they rehearse a tragedy about Pyramus and Thisbe to perform at a royal wedding.
tossups.r: Their leading man, the weaver Nick Bottom, is given a donkey’s head by the trickster fairy Puck. In the nearby forest, four young Athenians are thrown into confusion by a magic love potion. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the fairy queen Titania.

tossups.p: In this play, a fairy’s mistake causes a young man named Lysander to abandon his beloved Hermia and fall instead for his rival’s former love, Helena. The fairy king Oberon eventually orders the mix-up corrected so that both Athenian couples can marry happily.
tossups.r: That same fairy, Puck, also transforms a weaver named Nick Bottom by giving him a donkey’s head while he rehearses a play with his fellow “rude mechanicals.” For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy that ends with a triple wedding presided over by Theseus.

tossups.p: This play opens with the Duke of Athens impatiently awaiting his wedding to Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons, in four days’ time. Their marriage celebration at the end of the play includes a disastrous performance of Pyramus and Thisbe.
tossups.r: That tragedy is performed by a troupe of “rude mechanicals” led by Peter Quince, whose star actor Nick Bottom spends much of the play wearing a donkey’s head. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy in which the fairy Puck confuses two pairs of young lovers with a magic potion.

tossups.p: This play’s mischievous sprite is also known as Robin Goodfellow, a trickster figure from English folklore. Acting on the fairy king Oberon’s orders, he smears the juice of a magic flower on a sleeping Athenian’s eyelids.
tossups.r: He means to fix Demetrius’s feelings for Helena but enchants Lysander instead, confusing both young men, and the same fairy later gives a weaver named Nick Bottom the head of a donkey. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy featuring the fairy queen Titania.

tossups.p: This play’s amateur actors choose to rehearse in the forest at night so curious townspeople will not discover their secret play. There, their leading man is transformed by a mischievous fairy into a creature with a donkey’s head.
tossups.r: That same fairy, Puck, had already confused two Athenian men into chasing the same woman with a magic love potion, and Nick Bottom, the transformed weaver, briefly becomes the object of the fairy queen Titania’s affection. For 10 points, name this Shakespeare comedy that also features the fairy king Oberon.

trap.title: Not just “dreams”
trap.body: A few tossups are actually about the broader idea of dreams (quoting lines like Puck’s epilogue or Prospero’s “we are such stuff as dreams are made on” from _The Tempest_) and only accept this play’s title as one possible answer among several. If the clues list several unrelated works about dreaming before narrowing down, the judges may want the single word “dreams,” not this specific play.
trap.fix: Wait for a giveaway that names Shakespeare, Puck, Bottom, or the Athenian lovers by name — that confirms the real answer is this play, not the general topic of dreams.
trap.line: Real answer line: A Midsummer Night’s Dream (also accept it without “A”).

topics.name: Ulysses
topics.kicker: Joyce’s modernist novel · One Dublin day echoing Homer’s Odyssey
topics.briefing: On June 16, 1904, an ordinary Dublin ad salesman named Leopold Bloom wanders the city buying soap, attending a funeral, and quietly worrying about his wife Molly’s afternoon visitor. James Joyce turned that single ordinary day into one of the most ambitious novels ever written, loosely retelling Homer’s _Odyssey_ scene by scene. _Ulysses_ made the stream of consciousness style famous, pouring its characters’ raw thoughts straight onto the page, and fans still celebrate June 16 every year as “Bloomsday.”

tossups.p: This novel opens with the line “Stately, plump Buck Mulligan came from the stairhead, bearing a bowl of lather.” That same morning, Mulligan argues with his gloomy roommate, a young teacher and poet named Stephen Dedalus.
tossups.r: Elsewhere in Dublin, an advertising canvasser named Leopold Bloom spends the day attending a funeral, eating a kidney for breakfast, and worrying about his wife’s plans to meet another man. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel set on a single day in 1904.

tossups.p: One character in this novel tells his employer that “history is a nightmare from which I am trying to awake” during a conversation in which that headmaster makes antisemitic remarks. That character, Stephen Dedalus, is still mourning his mother’s recent death.
tossups.r: Meanwhile, Leopold Bloom wanders Dublin thinking about his wife Molly’s afternoon visitor, Blazes Boylan. The novel ends with Molly’s long unpunctuated monologue, which repeats the word “yes.” For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel set on June 16, 1904.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist writes to a woman named Martha Clifford under the pen name Henry Flower. That protagonist, Leopold Bloom, picks up her reply at the post office before continuing his errands around Dublin.
tossups.r: Bloom spends the day avoiding his house, since he knows his wife Molly is expecting a visit from Blazes Boylan. The novel’s final chapter is Molly’s famous soliloquy, ending with the word “yes.” For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel narrating a single day in Dublin.

tossups.p: In one chapter of this novel, a fiercely nationalist character called the Citizen argues with the protagonist at Barney Kiernan’s pub and hurls a biscuit tin at him as he leaves. That chapter’s exaggerated, mock-heroic style parodies old Irish legends.
tossups.r: The protagonist of this novel, Leopold Bloom, faces prejudice because he is Jewish throughout the book. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel that also follows the young writer Stephen Dedalus through Dublin on a single day.

tossups.p: A chapter of this novel set on Sandymount Strand follows the protagonist’s thoughts as he watches a young woman named Gerty MacDowell on the beach. That chapter imitates the sentimental style of romance novels.
tossups.r: The protagonist, advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom, spends the day avoiding home, since his wife Molly is expecting Blazes Boylan. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel set in Dublin on June 16, 1904.

tossups.p: One chapter of this novel is broken up with newspaper-style headlines as its characters debate rhetoric inside a Dublin newspaper office. Another chapter mimics the historical development of English prose style across centuries.
tossups.r: The novel as a whole loosely retells Homer’s _Odyssey_, with ad canvasser Leopold Bloom standing in for the wandering hero and his wife Molly standing in for the faithful Penelope. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel.

tossups.p: A 1933 court ruling by judge John Woolsey lifted a long obscenity ban on this novel in the United States, after an earlier magazine serialization had led to a similar court case. It had first been published in full in Paris in 1922 by Sylvia Beach’s bookshop, Shakespeare and Company.
tossups.r: The novel follows Leopold Bloom and the young writer Stephen Dedalus through Dublin on a single day, echoing Homer’s _Odyssey_. For 10 points, name this stream-of-consciousness novel by James Joyce.

tossups.p: Fans of this novel celebrate its setting every year on June 16, a holiday nicknamed after one of its characters. Celebrants often eat the same lunch its protagonist does, a Gorgonzola cheese sandwich at a Dublin pub called Davy Byrne’s.
tossups.r: That protagonist, Leopold Bloom, spends the day avoiding home while his wife Molly expects a visit from Blazes Boylan. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel, whose title alludes to Homer’s wandering hero.

tossups.p: This novel’s final chapter is a long, nearly unpunctuated monologue spoken by a woman recalling her husband’s marriage proposal and ending with the word “yes” repeated several times. That woman, Molly Bloom, has spent the afternoon with her lover Blazes Boylan.
tossups.r: Molly’s husband, Leopold Bloom, spends the novel wandering Dublin while young writer Stephen Dedalus deals with his own troubles. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel set on a single day in 1904.

tossups.p: Throughout this novel, its protagonist grows increasingly anxious about his wife’s planned afternoon meeting with a boastful concert promoter named Blazes Boylan. He distracts himself with errands, a funeral, and a stop at a pub for lunch.
tossups.r: That protagonist, Leopold Bloom, shares the spotlight with young writer Stephen Dedalus, who begins the novel arguing with his roommate Buck Mulligan. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel set in Dublin on a single day in June 1904.

tossups.p: One character in this novel scribbles a short poem on a scrap torn from the headmaster Mr. Deasy’s letter about cattle disease. That character, Stephen Dedalus, had promised to help get Deasy’s letter printed in a newspaper.
tossups.r: Meanwhile, a man named Bantam Lyons mistakes something Leopold Bloom says about a newspaper for a hot tip on a horse race. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel following Stephen and Bloom through Dublin on a single day.

tossups.p: In one scene of this novel, a character notices the letters “I.N.R.I.” or “I.H.S.” embroidered on the back of a priest’s vestments and wonders what they mean. That same character later visits the Freeman’s Journal office to arrange an advertisement for a merchant named Keyes.
tossups.r: This novel’s protagonist, Leopold Bloom, spends the day thinking about his wife Molly’s afternoon visitor, Blazes Boylan. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel that ends with Molly’s soliloquy.

tossups.p: Though the published text does not print them, this novel’s eighteen chapters are traditionally nicknamed after episodes of Homer’s _Odyssey_, such as “Calypso,” “Nausicaa,” and “Penelope.” Critics use these nicknames to describe the novel’s shifting styles, which range from newspaper headlines to a play script.
tossups.r: The novel’s Odysseus figure, Leopold Bloom, wanders Dublin on a single day while his wife Molly, standing in for Penelope, waits at home. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel.

tossups.p: This novel’s protagonist is a Jewish Dubliner who faces casual antisemitism from several characters over the course of a single day, including an argument at a pub that ends with a thrown biscuit tin. He is also haunted by the death of his infant son, Rudy, years earlier.
tossups.r: That protagonist, advertising canvasser Leopold Bloom, shares the novel with a young writer named Stephen Dedalus. For 10 points, name this James Joyce novel that ends with wife Molly Bloom’s famous soliloquy.

tossups.p: This novel famously pours characters’ raw, often unpunctuated thoughts directly onto the page, as in Stephen Dedalus’s musings on Sandymount Strand and its closing chapter narrated by Molly Bloom. T. S. Eliot called it one of the most important books of its era.
tossups.r: Leopold Bloom, the novel’s Odysseus-like hero, spends the day wandering Dublin while Molly awaits a visit from Blazes Boylan. For 10 points, name this stream-of-consciousness novel by James Joyce.

trap.title: Which “Ulysses”?
trap.body: Three different things share this title: Homer’s Greek hero Odysseus (whose Latin name is Ulysses), Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s 1833 poem about that hero’s old age (“To strive, to seek, to find, and not to yield”), and James Joyce’s 1922 novel. Clues about Troy, the Cyclops, Penelope, or Ithaca usually point to the mythological hero or Tennyson’s poem, not this novel. Also watch out for Ulysses S. Grant, the Civil War general and U.S. president.
trap.fix: Wait for clues naming Leopold Bloom, Molly, Stephen Dedalus, Dublin, or June 16, 1904 — those confirm the answer is Joyce’s novel, not the myth, the poem, or the president.
trap.line: Real answer line: Ulysses (reject Odysseus and Ulysses S. Grant).

tossups.p: As a boy, this novella’s narrator was fascinated by the blank, unexplored spaces on maps, dreaming of someday exploring them himself. As an adult, he takes a job piloting a steamboat for an ivory-trading company instead.
tossups.r: That narrator, Charles Marlow, journeys up a great river in search of a company agent whose dying words are “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this novella by Joseph Conrad.

tossups.p: This novella’s frame story takes place aboard a ship called the Nellie, anchored on the Thames estuary at dusk. There, the sailor Charles Marlow begins telling his companions about a strange job piloting a steamboat.
tossups.r: Marlow’s steamboat carries him up the Congo River in search of an ivory agent named Kurtz. For 10 points, name this novella by Joseph Conrad.

tossups.p: Before this novella begins, a Danish captain named Fresleven dies in a dispute with villagers, which is how its narrator gets hired to replace him. That narrator, Charles Marlow, later pilots a steamboat up a great river for the same trading company.
tossups.r: Marlow searches for an increasingly unstable agent named Kurtz, whose final words are “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella.

tossups.p: This novella’s central figure writes a report for a society devoted to “suppressing savage customs,” then scrawls a chilling postscript on it reading “Exterminate all the brutes!” That figure, an ivory agent named Kurtz, has set himself up as a feared ruler deep in the interior.
tossups.r: Sent to find him, the sailor Charles Marlow pilots a steamboat up the Congo River. For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella whose central figure dies murmuring “The horror! The horror!”

tossups.p: A young Russian man whose patchwork clothing makes him look like a harlequin greets this novella’s narrator at the Inner Station. That devoted follower idolizes the ivory agent he serves, even after witnessing his cruelty.
tossups.r: The narrator, Charles Marlow, has come to retrieve that agent, Kurtz, whose last words are “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this novella in which Marlow journeys up the Congo River, by Joseph Conrad.

tossups.p: At the end of this novella, its narrator visits a grieving woman known only as “the Intended” and lies to her about her fiancé’s final words. That fiancé, an ivory agent named Kurtz, had actually died whispering “The horror! The horror!”
tossups.r: The narrator, Charles Marlow, had piloted a steamboat up the Congo River to find Kurtz. For 10 points, name this novella by Joseph Conrad.

tossups.p: In his essay “An Image of Africa,” the novelist Chinua Achebe accused this novella’s author of racism for how it portrays African characters. Despite that critique, the book is still widely read and taught as an attack on European colonialism.
tossups.r: Its narrator, sailor Charles Marlow, journeys up the Congo River searching for an ivory agent named Kurtz. For 10 points, name this novella by Joseph Conrad.

tossups.p: This novella’s narrator compares the European city that houses his trading company’s headquarters to a “whited sepulchre.” He then sets sail for Africa to pilot a steamboat up a great river.
tossups.r: That narrator, Charles Marlow, searches for an ivory agent named Kurtz, whose dying words are “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella.

tossups.p: Before this novella’s narrator departs for Africa, a company doctor measures his skull and warns him to avoid irritation even more than the sun. That narrator, Charles Marlow, later pilots a steamboat up the Congo River.
tossups.r: He searches for an ivory agent named Kurtz, who has made himself a feared, god-like ruler in the interior. For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella whose central figure dies saying “The horror! The horror!”

tossups.p: This novella’s narrator sarcastically nicknames the greedy, ivory-hungry company agents he travels with “pilgrims.” He watches them ignore the exhausted, starving laborers that the company has forced to work for it.
tossups.r: That narrator, Charles Marlow, pilots a steamboat up the Congo River to find an ivory agent named Kurtz. For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella.

tossups.p: This novella’s narrator waits in frustration at a company station for rivets needed to repair his damaged steamboat. Once it is fixed, he finally continues his journey up a great river.
tossups.r: He is searching for an ivory agent named Kurtz, who dies murmuring “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this novella in which Charles Marlow travels up the Congo River, by Joseph Conrad.

tossups.p: A greedy group called the Eldorado Exploring Expedition sets off into the interior of this novella’s setting searching for treasure, and simply vanishes. Its narrator later meets a wandering young Russian who has become a devoted admirer of Kurtz.
tossups.r: The narrator, Charles Marlow, pilots a steamboat up the Congo River to find Kurtz, who dies saying “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella.

tossups.p: This novella’s narrator is described sitting “in the pose of a meditating Buddha” when he finishes telling his story to companions aboard a ship called the Nellie. He says he cannot truly share his experience, because “we live, as we dream—alone.”
tossups.r: That narrator, Charles Marlow, recalls piloting a steamboat up the Congo River to find an ivory agent named Kurtz. For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella.

tossups.p: This novella loosely inspired the film _Apocalypse Now_, which relocates its plot to the Vietnam War, and a line announcing its central figure’s death is the epigraph of T. S. Eliot’s poem “The Hollow Men.” The film also borrows that character’s famous dying words.
tossups.r: Those words, “The horror! The horror!”, are spoken by the dying ivory agent Kurtz aboard the narrator Charles Marlow’s steamboat. For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella set along the Congo River.

tossups.p: This novella was first serialized in _Blackwood’s Magazine_ in 1899 before being published as a book in 1902. It was written by a Polish-born sailor turned novelist.
tossups.r: The story follows Charles Marlow as he pilots a steamboat up the Congo River searching for the ivory agent Kurtz, who dies saying “The horror! The horror!” For 10 points, name this Joseph Conrad novella.

clues.t: Charles Marlow travels up the Congo River aboard a steamboat for an ivory-trading company
Dying ivory agent Kurtz’s last words are “The horror! The horror!”
Written by the Polish-British novelist Joseph Conrad, first serialized in 1899
Kurtz’s report ends with a scrawled postscript reading “Exterminate all the brutes!”
A frame story set aboard the ship Nellie, anchored on the Thames, introduces the whole tale
Marlow lies to Kurtz’s grieving fiancee, known only as “the Intended,” about his final words
A devoted Russian follower of Kurtz, whose patchwork clothes make him look like a harlequin, aids Marlow
Critic Chinua Achebe’s essay “An Image of Africa” accused this novella’s author of racism
Marlow compares Brussels, the company’s headquarters city, to a “whited sepulchre”
As a boy, Marlow was fascinated by the blank spaces on unexplored maps
A Danish captain named Fresleven died in a dispute before Marlow took over his post
At the Central Station, Marlow finds a painting Kurtz made of a blindfolded woman carrying a torch
The novella condemns European colonialism as, in Marlow’s words, little more than “robbery with violence”
Its plot loosely inspired the film _Apocalypse Now_, which moves the story to the Vietnam War; some tournaments rule that title a wrong answer here
Kurtz appears in an epigraph (“Mistah Kurtz—he dead”) in T. S. Eliot’s poem “The Hollow Men”
A company doctor measures Marlow’s skull before his voyage and warns him to avoid irritation even more than the sun
Marlow sarcastically nicknames the greedy, ivory-hungry company agents he travels with “pilgrims”
Marlow waits in frustration at the Central Station for rivets to repair his damaged steamboat
Marlow is described sitting “in the pose of a meditating Buddha” after telling his story
Marlow says “we live, as we dream—alone,” frustrated that his listeners cannot understand
A greedy group called the Eldorado Exploring Expedition searches the interior for treasure and vanishes
Kurtz was originally sent into the interior by the trading company on a mission to “civilize” the region
First serialized in _Blackwood’s Magazine_ before being published as a book in 1902

trap.title: Not “Apocalypse Now”
trap.body: Francis Ford Coppola’s film _Apocalypse Now_ borrows this novella’s plot and even Kurtz’s dying words, but moves the setting to the Vietnam War. At least one real tournament specifically ruled that the film’s title should not be accepted for this novella’s answer line.
trap.fix: Listen for the setting — the Congo River, Marlow, or the ship Nellie mean this novella; Vietnam, Captain Willard, or Colonel Kurtz mean the film.
trap.line: Real answer line: Heart of Darkness (reject “Apocalypse Now”).
